excerpt: Georgia and South Carolina are both at-fault states, not no-fault. What that means for who pays after a crash, and how shared fault affects recovery.
keyTakeaways: Georgia and South Carolina are both fault states where the at-fault driver pays for damages, unlike no-fault states that use PIP coverage. Georgia bars recovery at 50% fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); South Carolina bars at 51% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Georgia's statute of limitations is two years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33); South Carolina allows three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Understanding these rules is critical to maximizing your car accident recovery.

faqs.question: Is Georgia a fault or no-fault state for car accidents?
faqs.answer: Georgia is a fault state. The driver who caused the accident is financially responsible for the injured party's damages, including medical expenses, lost wages, property damage, and pain and suffering. Injured parties can file a claim with the at-fault driver's insurer or sue directly in civil court.

faqs.question: Is South Carolina a fault or no-fault state?
faqs.answer: South Carolina is a fault state, similar to Georgia. The at-fault driver's liability insurance covers the injured party's damages. South Carolina also requires uninsured motorist (UM) coverage on every auto policy (S.C. Code § 38-77-150), which cannot be rejected, providing extra protection when at-fault drivers lack insurance.

faqs.question: What is the difference between fault and no-fault car insurance?
faqs.answer: In a fault state, you file a claim against the at-fault driver's insurance. In a no-fault state, you file with your own insurer through Personal Injury Protection (PIP) coverage regardless of who caused the crash. No-fault states restrict your right to sue unless injuries meet a severity or monetary threshold.

faqs.question: How does comparative fault work in Georgia and South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Both states use modified comparative fault. In Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), you recover nothing if 50% or more at fault. In South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.), you recover nothing if 51% or more at fault. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault — so 30% fault on a $100,000 claim yields $70,000.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a car accident claim in Georgia and South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Georgia has a two-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina allows three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines permanently bars your ability to file a lawsuit, so it is critical to act promptly.

faqs.question: Can I buy PIP insurance in Georgia even though it is a fault state?
faqs.answer: Not as PIP. Georgia does not require PIP and Georgia insurers sell Medical Payments (MedPay) coverage instead — an optional coverage that pays medical expenses for you and your passengers regardless of fault, up to the limit you choose. It does not replace lost wages; those are recovered from the at-fault driver's liability insurer.
